units.text: DETERMINING SURFACES BY SHORT CURVES AND APPLICATIONS
Introduction

In this article, a closed hyperbolic surface S means a closed surface equipped with a hyperbolic metric.By the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, S has genus g ≥ 2.Moreover, S is geometrically equivalent to a quotient G\H, where H denotes the hyperbolic plane and G is a cocompact torsion-free discrete subgroup of the Lie group H = SL(2, R).
Here we are mainly interested in the interplay between the hyperbolic geometry of the quotient and the arithmetic of the group G.

For any integer g ≥ 2, let M g be the moduli space of closed hyperbolic surfaces of genus g and consider the respective Teichmuller space T g .It is known that for any g ≥ 2 there exists 6g − 4 marked simple curves on the surface of genus g such that any element in T g is uniquely determined by lengths of respective simple closed geodesics homotopic to these simples curves [20].It is a natural problem to find for any marked surface S ∈ T g a parametrization by lengths of closed geodesics whose values in S are the smallest possible.

If we consider a marked surface S with injectivity radius s > 0, it is possible to determine 9g − 9 simple closed geodesics from a short pants decomposition of the surface which parameterize T g and such that these lengths of the geodesics on S are bounded by a linear function Ag + B, where A is universal and B depends only on s (see [8,Proposition 4.1.7]).

Now we are able to improve the linear bound on g by a logarithmic bound.The main difference in this new construction is that we replace the classical pants decomposition by a decomposition in curves and arcs introduced by Parlier in [18].For a closed marked curve β in a marked hyperbolic surface S, the length of the unique closed geodesic in S homotopic to β is denoted by L β (S).In Section 3 we will prove the following theorem: Theorem 1.1.Given s > 0, for any marked closed hyperbolic surface S ∈ T g with injectivity radius at least s, there exist finitely many marked closed curves γ 1 , . . ., γ n in S with n ≤ 15g − 15 such that:
(1) L γ i (S) ≤ 20 log(4g) + 8 arcsinh
1 sinh( s 2 )
for all i = 1, . . ., n;
(2) The map T g → R n whose coordinates are given by the corresponding length functions L γ 1 , . . ., L γn is injective.

We remark that in some sense this result is optimal.Indeed, there exists a sequence of genera {g i } with lim i→∞ g i = ∞ such that we can find a closed hyperbolic surface S i of genus g i with ℓ(γ) ≥ 4  3 log(g i ) for all closed geodesic γ of S i (see [13,Theorem 1.10]).These examples imply that the upper bound of the theorem can be improved only in the constants.Moreover, given a marked topological pants decomposition P of a closed surface, for any set of marked closed curves which parameterize T g , at least one of them, namely γ, should intersect transversally some curve of P. Hence, if a marked hyperbolic surface S satisfies L η (S) ≤ ϵ for all η ∈ P, then by the Collar Lemma (see [4,Corollary 4.1.2])we have L γ (S) ≥ arcsinh 1 sinh( ϵ 2 ) , which can be very large for ϵ sufficiently small.Thus we can not remove the dependence on s.
The theorem above will be our main tool in two quantitative results about arithmetic and semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.The precise definition of these objects will be given in Subsection 2.2.

Firstly, we recall that if we fix a hyperbolic surface S of genus 2, for any g > 2 there exist finitely many points in M g which are coverings of S. Hence there exists a minimal distance δ S (g), concerning Teichmuller metric, among all such coverings of genus g.However, it follows from the proof of the Ehrenpreis conjecture given by Kahn-Markovic ( [11]) that δ S (g) goes to 0 when g grows.It does not follow directly from their proof in a quantitative way how this function goes to 0 for a general surface S.

In Subsection 4.1 we will combine the pivotal property of minimal spacing (see Lemma 4.1 or [15]) of suitable arithmetic groups with Theorem 1.1 in order to show the following theorem, which says that for arithmetic surfaces the function δ S (g) is bounded below by a polynomial function on 1/g.Theorem 1.2.Let S be an arithmetic hyperbolic surface.There exists a constant A depending only on S such that the Teichmuller distance of any two surfaces S ′ , S ′′ ∈ M g which cover S is bounded below by A g 240 .

We expect, by our proof of the theorem above and the sharpness of the Theorem 1.1, that there is no a better bound than polynomial.Indeed, this would be true if the following question has positive answer which can be seen as a quantitative form of the Ehrenpreis conjecture.Question 1. Do there exist, for any hyperbolic surface S, a polynomial Q depending only on S such that δ S (g) ≤ Q(1/g)?

It follows from a result of Borel [3] that for any g ≥ 2 there exist only finitely many arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces in M g .Since arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces are rare, it is natural to generalize the notion of arithmeticity in such way that we can find a larger set of examples and that the number theory continues giving geometric results.Among all generalizations, the probably most studied has been the one given in [19] by Schaller and Wolfart, where it was defined semi-arithmetic groups (see definition in Subsection 2.2) by a slightly (but important) change in the definition of Fuchsian arithmetic groups.Very recently, various aspects of these groups have been explored in connections with multiple objects of mathematics (see for example [6], [10], [14], [17]).

Once we have defined a semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surface, we have naturally a geometric invariant (the genus) and an arithmetic invariant (the degree of the invariant trace field).In [1], a new more intricate invariant is defined, namely stretch, and the main result in [op.cit] implies that there are only finitely many examples of surfaces with these invariants bounded.We recall that any arithmetic hyperbolic surface is semi-arithmetic with stretch 1.
It is possible to deduce from [2] that for any d fixed, if AS g,d denotes the set of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with degree of the invariant trace field at most d, then (1) lim
g→∞ log #AS g,d g log g = 2

The tools used in [2] in order to obtain (1) do not apply to non-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.Nevertheless, we are able to count semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces using the arithmetic nature of the exponential of lengths of closed geodesics.Indeed, these numbers are always unit integers of some number field.Moreover, if we take the length of some closed geodesic, the degree of such field and the stretch give bound to the coefficients of the minimal polynomial of its exponential over Q.We will apply our first geometric theorem in Subsection 4.2 for embedding a set of semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces in a list of finite integers polynomials to obtain the following general estimate.Furthermore, the constant C satisfies C ≤ U Ld 2 for some universal constant U > 0.
Preliminaries

2.1.The geometry of the moduli spaces.In this subsection, we review the classical definitions of the Teichmuller and Moduli spaces of closed hyperbolic surfaces.Our references are [4] and [9].A closed hyperbolic surface of genus g ≥ 2 is a closed surface S with g handles equipped with a Riemannian metric of constant curvature −1.For a closed hyperbolic surface S, its injectivity radius r > 0 it is equal to one half of its systole sys(S), i.e. r = 1  2 sys(S) = 1 2 min{ℓ(γ)} where γ runs through all closed geodesics in S. If we fix a closed surface R of genus g, a marked hyperbolic surface is a pair (S, ϕ) where ϕ : R → S is a homeomorphism.We say that two marked surfaces (S, ϕ) and (S ′ , ϕ ′ ) are equivalent if there exists an isometry m : S → S ′ such that ϕ ′ and m • ϕ are isotopic.The set of equivalence classes is known as Teichmuller space and denoted by T g .

It follows from two theorems of Teichmuller that for any pair (S, ϕ), (S ′ , ϕ ′ ) of marked hyperbolic surfaces, there exists a unique quasiconformal homeomorphism h : S → S ′ (see [9, §11.1.2]for quasiconformal maps definition) of minimum dilation K h among all homeomorphisms f : S → S ′ such that ϕ ′ is homotopic to f • ϕ (see [9,Theorems 11.8 and 11.9]).We define the Teichmuller distance between the pair of marked surfaces (S, ϕ) and (S ′ , ϕ ′ ) by 1  2 log(K h ).The moduli space M g of hyperbolic surfaces of genus g is the set of equivalence classes of hyperbolic surfaces with respect to isometries.Let S, S ′ be representative points in M g , we define the Teichmuller distance of the classes of S and S ′ , denoted by d T (S, S ′ ), as the minimal of all distances of marked surfaces which represent the respective points (see [9,Section 12.3]).We note that we can suppose, replacing S ′ by an isometric copy of it if necessary, that the mapping h preserves marking, i.e. if d T (S, S ′ ) is the Teichmuller distance between (S, ϕ) and (S ′ , ϕ ′ ), and h : S → S ′ realizes the distance, we can suppose that (ϕ ′ ) −1 • h • ϕ : R → R is isotopic to identity.

For any nontrivial free homotopy class [β] of closed curve in R, and marked hyperbolic surface (S, ϕ), the length of the unique closed geodesic homotopic to ϕ(β) with respect of the hyperbolic metric on S is denoted by L [β] (S).For abuse notation, for any closed curve β ⊂ R, and marked surface S, L β (S) means L [β] (S).We will call L β as a length function in T g .The length functions satisfy the following theorem (see [4,Theorem 6.4.3]).
Theorem 2.1.Let S, S ′ be closed hyperbolic surfaces of genus g ≥ 2. If a homeomorphism f : S → S ′ is K-quasiconformal, then for each closed geodesic β on S, the unique closed geodesic
f [β] in the homotopy class of f • β satisfies 1 K L β (S) ≤ L f [β] (S ′ ) ≤ KL β (S).

For future reference, we recall that by the classical Poincaré-Koebe uniformization theorem, every hyperbolic surface of genus at least 2 can be given as a quotient G\H, where G is a torsion-free Fuchsian group.
Semi-Arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.In this section, we will give the definitions of arithmetic and semi-arithmetic surfaces.The main references for what follows are [1], [3], [16] and [19].

We start by defining what a semi-arithmetic group is.Let G < SL(2, R) be a Fuchsian group, we say that G is cofinite if the quotient space G\H has finite area.We will denote by G (2) the group generated by the squares of the elements of G, i.e.G (2)
:= ⟨T 2 | T ∈ G⟩. The trace set of G is the set Tr(G) := {|tr(T )| | T ∈ G}. Finally, we define the invariant trace field of G to be F = Q(Tr(G (2) )) ⊂ R.

A cofinite Fuchsian group G is said to be semi-arithmetic if the invariant trace field is a totally real number field and Tr(G (2) ) is contained in the ring of integers O F of F .We note that any conjugated group and any finite index subgroup of a semi-arithmetic group is also semi-arithmetic with the same invariant trace field.

For G to be called an arithmetic group, it must be semi-arithmetic and satisfy the following condition: if ϕ is Q-monomorphism (or simply an embedding) from F to R, different from the identity, then ϕ(|tr(T )|) ∈ [−2, 2] for all T ∈ G (2) .

Let G be a semi-arithmetic group with invariant trace field F. Consider the F − subalgebra of the algebra M(2, R) of 2 × 2 real matrices, generated by G (2) .It turns out that this algebra is a quaternion algebra over F, namely the invariant quaternion algebra of G and denoted by A(G).Moreover, G (2) is contained in the group of elements of reduced norm one in an order O ⊂ A(G), i.e.G (2) ⊂ O 1 .We also note that A(G) does not depend, up to F isomorphism, of any conjugated or finite index subgroup of G.
It is well established (see [3] for example) that there exists an F −algebra morphism
ρ : A(G) → M(2, R) r for some r ≤ [F : Q] such that ρ(O 1

) is a cofinite discrete subgroup of isometries of the product H r .Since r depends only on A(G), we call it the arithmetic dimension of G.This name comes from the fact that for the arithmetic Fuchsian group, we have r = 1.

We define the stretch of G as the infimum of all L > 0 such that there exists a L−Lipschitz map f : H → H r , with respect to maximum metric on H r , such that f (T • z) = ρ(T ) • f (z) for all z ∈ H and T ∈ G (2) .It follows from the nature of ρ that L ≥ 1.Moreover, for arithmetic groups or triangle groups, we have L = 1.Hence, the arithmetic dimension and stretch measure how far a semi-arithmetic is from being arithmetic or triangular.

We say that a surface S ∈ M g is semi-arithmetic (respectively arithmetic) if S = G\H for some semi-arithmetic (respectively arithmetic) Fuchsian group G and we denote the set of such surfaces by SA g (respectively A g ).In particular, it is well defined the invariant trace field, invariant quaternion algebra (up to isomorphism), arithmetic dimension, and stretch of S in a natural way since these invariants do not depend on the conjugacy class of a semi-arithmetic Fuchsian group.

We conclude this subsection by recalling a relation between the geometry of a hyperbolic surface with its uniformizing group.Let G be a Fuchsian group, for each T ∈ G hyperbolic, i.e. with |tr(T )| > 2, we have a unique geodesic L T ⊂ H fixed by T where T acts as a translation of displacement ℓ(T ) and hence projects on a closed geodesic of same length on the quotient G\H.Conjugating T by a suitable element in SL(2, R) we can suppose that L T is the imaginary axis and then e ℓ(T ) = λ(T ), where λ(T ) is the absolute value of the biggest eigenvalue of T 2 .

Number theoretic facts about semi-arithmetic Fuchsian groups.Let α be an algebraic integer and consider its minimal polynomial P ∈ Z[X].We say that a complex number β is Galois conjugate to α if P (β) = 0.The house of α is the number α = max{|β| : β is Galois conjugate to α}.

We say that an algebraic integer α is reciprocal if it is Galois conjugate to its inverse.For a reciprocal number α, the set of roots of its minimal polynomial P is invariant by the map x → x −1 .Hence P has even degree and satisfies P (X) = X n P (1/X).Now we will give an extension of a proposition already proved in [1, Proposition 4.2].We will explore the arithmetic nature of eigenvalues of hyperbolic elements in semiarithmetic Fuchsian groups and we will give a systolic estimate for semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.Proposition 2.2.Let S be a semi-arithmetic closed hyperbolic surface of invariant trace field of degree at most d and stretch at most L, then:

(1) For any closed geodesic β ⊂ S, the number e ℓ(β) is a reciprocal algebraic integer of degree at most 2d and house at most e ℓ(β)L .(2) There exists some constant s > 0 which depends only on d and L such that S has injectivity radius at least s.
Proof.We can write S = G\H for some semi-arithmetic Fuchsian group.As we have mentioned before, Since e ±ℓ(β) are the roots of the polynomial
X 2 − tr(T (β) 2 )X + 1 ∈ O F [X]
, we conclude that e ℓ(β) is a real reciprocal algebraic integer of degree bounded above by 2d.The estimate of the house of e ℓ(β) follows from [1, Proposition 3.3] and this proves (1).

For (2) it is sufficient to give a lower bound for all closed geodesics of X.By Dimitrov's proof of Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture [7, Theorem 1], we have λ(T (β)) > 2 1 4d .Thus, for any closed geodesic β ⊂ S it holds
ℓ(β) = log(λ(T (β)) L ) L ≥ log( λ(T (β)) ) L ≥ log(2) 4dL .

We finish this subsection with a lemma which counts the number of reciprocal algebraic integers with an upper bound on degree and house.Let U m (X) be the set of real reciprocal algebraic integers with degree at most 2m and house bounded by X.
Lemma 2.3.Given positive integer m and a number X > 1, the set U m (X) is finite with at most 2m(4mX) m 2 elements.

Length coordinates with logarithmic bound

Let S ∈ M g be a closed hyperbolic surface of genus g ≥ 2. We denote by d the hyperbolic distance on S and for any set U of closed geodesics or arcs in S, ℓ(U) denotes the set of their respective lengths {ℓ(u) : u ∈ U}.We can decompose S into curves Γ = {γ 1 , . . ., γ k } and arcs A = {a 1 , . . ., a m } so that S \ {Γ, A} is a collection of geodesic right angled hexagons.

For each curve γ ∈ Γ we fix the choice of two arcs that have one endpoint in γ, one arc on each side of γ.Let's call such endpoints p − γ and p + γ .Thus, we can define the twist parameter of γ, denoted by τ (γ), as the oriented distance of p − γ and p + γ , ie,
|τ (γ)| = d(p − γ , p + γ )

. The surface S is uniquely determined by the twist parameters of each γ ∈ Γ, and by the lengths of the decomposition arcs, that is, by the sets τ (Γ) = {τ (γ 1 ), . . ., τ (γ k )} and ℓ(A) ([18, Lemma 3.4]).However, the surface can be determined just by the twist parameter of each γ ∈ Γ and the length of some closed curves in S. For this, let's define a new class of curves.

Given a ∈ A and an orientation on S \ Γ, this defines an orientation on the boundary curves of S \ Γ that are at the ends of a, say γ 1 and γ 2 .Take γ a to be the closed geodesic in the free homotopy class of γ 1 * a * γ 2 * a −1 .This curve will be called the chain associated with a. Thus, the surface S is uniquely determined by τ (Γ), ℓ(Γ) and ℓ(Γ A ) where Γ A = {γ a } a∈A ([18, Lemma 3.5]).We call the sets of curves Γ and Γ A the curve and chain system.

The next proposition is an adapted result from [18, Theorem 1.3].We will give a proof for reader convenience.For this, we recall two useful general lemmata (see [18, Lemma 2.6 and Lemma 3.8]).We recall that for any s > 0, the s−thick part of M g is the set M ≥s g formed by hyperbolic surfaces with injectivity radius at least s.Proposition 3.3.Given ε > 0, any surface S ∈ M ≥ε g admits a curve and chain system Γ, Γ A satisfying
ℓ(γ) < 2 log(4g) for all γ ∈ Γ ℓ(γ a ) < 8 log(4g) + 4 arcsinh 1 sinh( ε 2 ) for all a ∈ A ℓ(a) < 2 log(4g) + 2 arcsinh 1 sinh( ε 2 )
for all a ∈ A.
Furthermore, this curve and chain system can be chosen such that for any γ ∈ Γ and side of γ, there exists at least one arc a ∈ A joining γ to δ ∈ Γ with δ ̸ = γ.
Proof.The proof follows the same circle of ideas of [18,Theorem 1.3].For every x ∈ S we let δ x be the shortest nontrivial loop based on x.As the smallest loop, δ x satisfies the Lemma 3.1
ℓ(δ x ) < 2 • arccosh 1 2 sin π 12g−6 < 2 log(4g).
Now we consider the collection Γ of all simple closed geodesics in S which are free homotopic to δ x for some x ∈ S. Let Γ be a maximal disjoint set of Γ.
To construct the set of arcs for the desired decomposition, we start by considering a decomposition in Voronoi cells around the boundaries of S \ Γ.That is, the surface S is partitioned into sets

Furthermore, the amount of curves that determine the surface S is at most 15g − 15.

We finish this section with a lemma which will be useful in Subsection 4.2.We say that a family Ω of closed curves on a surface R gives a parametrization by a marked (topological) curve and chain system if Ω is obtained by a construction as in the proof of the theorem above.By definition Ω is constructed by a unique curve and chain system, which we will call the underlying curve and chain system of Ω.

Let F g be the set of all possible Ω ′ s for a surface of genus g up to the action of the group of homeomorphisms of R. Since this action on M g is trivial, then does not matter if we replace a curve and chain system on a surface by its image by a homeomorphism.But, topologically, the set of all systems can be decomposed into finitely many orbits.Now we are able to give a quantitative upper bound for #F g .Lemma 3.5.The set F g is finite and

Applications
Minimal distance between coverings of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.

Given a hyperbolic surface S, for any n > 1 the number of n-sheeted coverings of S is equal to the number of conjugacy classes of subgroups of index n of the Fuchsian group Γ which uniformizes S. On the other hand, for a finitely generated group, there exist finitely many subgroups of a given index.By the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, the set of points in M g which are coverings of S is equal to the number of m-sheeted coverings of S for some explicit m depending only g and the genus of S. Thus, it is well defined the function δ S given by δ S (g) = 0, if there not exists coverings of S of genus g min{d T ( S, S) : S, S ∈ M g are different coverings of S}, otherwise, where d T denotes the Teichmuller metric in M g .It follows from the work of Kahn and Markovic in [11], where they proved the Ehrenpreis conjecture, that for any ε > 0 there exist different coverings of a fixed surface S with Teichmuller distance at most ε.Hence, lim g→∞ δ S (g) = 0 for any S.

It would be interesting if there would exist a uniform (qualitative) upper bound of all such functions.For example, is there a polynomial Q depending only on S such that δ S (g) ≤ Q(1/g)?If the answer is positive then this is the better which we can obtain due to our next theorem.Before it, we will recall the following Lemma -originally proved in [15, Lemma 2.1] -whose proof is simple and captures a strong particularity of arithmetic surfaces.

For any closed geodesic β on a hyperbolic surface S = Λ\H, let T β (S) ∈ Λ be a hyperbolic element such that its axis projects on β.It follows from (2) that the length ℓ β (S) and tr(T β (S)) are related by the equality:

Counting semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces.In the previous subsection we have used the fact that for any given totally real number field F , there exist finitely many arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces with invariant trace field F of a fixed genus.This fact is no longer true for semi-arithmetic surfaces.Indeed, in [6] it is shown that for any g ≥ 2 there exists a family of semi-arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with the same invariant trace field and arbitrarily small injectivity radius.However, if we bound the arithmetic dimension and stretch we have a picture similar to the arithmetic case.

For any integer r ≥ 1 and positive number L ≥ 1, we define the set SA g (r, L) = {S ∈ SA g | a.dim(S) ≤ r and δ(S) ≤ L}, where a.dim(S) is the arithmetic dimension of S and δ(S) is the stretch of S. In [1], it is shown that SA g (r, L) is always finite.In particular, for any d ≥ 1, there exist finitely many semi-arithmetic closed hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with bounded stretch and invariant trace field of degree at most d, since the arithmetic dimension is bounded above by the degree of the invariant trace field.We define now the set SA[g, d, L] of semi-arithmetic closed hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with invariant trace field of degree at most d and stretch at most L. We note that the set of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces of genus g with invariant trace field of degree at most d, denoted by AS g,d , is always a subset of SA[g, d, L] for any L ≥ 1.

Now we fix the well known Bolza surface [12], which is an arithmetic hyperbolic surface of genus 2 with quadratic invariant trace field.Hence, the number of coverings with genus g of the Bolza surface gives a lower bound for SA[g, d, L] for any L ≥ 1 and d ≥ 2. We note that it can be traced back from the proof of [2, Corollary 1.4] that (7) #SA[g, d, L] ≥ (bg) 2g
